1.1 The basic vocabulary

We start by introducing the basic vocabulary of synthetic category theory, taking inspiration from naive set theory. In the same way that functions between sets are taken as a primitive notion in naive set theory, as opposed to being defined via their graph, we similarly take functors between categories as a primitive notion, together with the basic relations they should satisfy.

In synthetic category theory, the role of collections is played by animae rather than sets. The principal distinction between sets and animae is that an identification between objects of an anima is structure rather than a mere property. Such identifications should therefore themselves form a collection of mathematical objects, hence an anima.

We initially treat animae as a primitive distinguished class of categories, leaving their structural characterization among categories unspecified. In the next chapter, we identify the groupoids among all categories and demand that a category is an anima precisely when it is a groupoid.

Epistemic status: The choice of foundational language introduced here is still evolving, and has become more and more refined over time. It was obtained by starting with the language of ‘naive category theory’ used by modern homotopy theorists, and refining it over time by adding more coherences whenever the need became transparent. We expect the current list of axiomatized coherences to be still incomplete, and our natural language treatment should not be thought of as an attempt of a full formalization of synthetic category theory.

1.1.1 Categories, functors and natural isomorphisms

Axiom A.1. The following are the primitives in the vocabulary of synthetic category theory:

(1)

There are categories, which we denote by symbols like \(C\), \(D\), and \(E\). Among categories, there are animae; these encode the idea of a homotopy-coherent collection.

(3)

Given parallel functors \(f,g\colon C\to D\), there is an anima \((f\cong g)\). For \(h\colon D\to E\) and \(k\colon B\to C\), there are functors \[ h\star -\colon (f\cong g)\to (hf\cong hg), \qquad -\star k\colon (f\cong g)\to (fk\cong gk), \] called postwhiskering and prewhiskering, respectively. There is also an inverse functor \[ (-)^{-1}\colon (f\cong g)\to (g\cong f). \]

Definition 1.1.1 (Terms). A functor \(f\colon C\to D\) may be displayed in term notation as \[ x:C\vdash f(x):D. \] The functor and the expression \(f(x)\) are two notations for the same datum. We call \(x:C\) its context. More generally, we may write \(C\vdash t:D\) when the name of the variable is left implicit.

Definition 1.1.2 (Absolute object). An absolute object \(c:C\) of a category \(C\) is a functor \(c\colon *\to C\). We sometimes also write \(c\in C\). An isomorphism between absolute objects \(c,c':C\) is a natural isomorphism between the functors \(c,c'\colon *\to C\).

Two natural isomorphisms are themselves parallel functors, so that their identifications again form an anima. The same construction may be iterated. We may display \(\alpha \) in term notation as \[ x:C\vdash \alpha (x):f(x)\cong g(x). \] This means a natural isomorphism of the two functors \(f\) and \(g\). The same convention applies to identifications between natural isomorphisms. The notation \(\cong \) for identifications is used to evoke the idea of isomorphisms in category theory. The following principle guides our use of this language:

Fundamental principle of homotopy theory: Whenever we would like to express that two things are equal, we should remember how they are equal by specifying an identification between them.

Definition 1.1.4 (Equivalence of categories). A functor \(f\colon C \to D\) is said to be an equivalence if there exists another functor \(g\colon D \to C\) equipped with natural isomorphisms \(\id _{C} \cong gf\) and \(\id _{D} \cong fg\). We refer to \(g\) as the inverse of \(f\). Equivalences will often be introduced by writing \(f\colon C \iso D\). We may write \(C \simeq D\) to indicate that \(C\) and \(D\) are equivalent via an unnamed equivalence.

Agda Equivalence data

Axiom A.2 (Terminal category). There is an anima \(*\), called the terminal category. For every category \(T\), there is a functor \(p_T\colon T\to *\). For any functors \(f,g\colon T\to *\), the functor \[ p_{(f\cong g)}\colon (f\cong g)\longrightarrow * \] is an equivalence.

Definition 1.1.5 (Constant functor). Let \(C\) and \(D\) be categories and let \(x\) be an absolute object of \(D\). We define the constant functor \(\const _x\colon C \to D\) as the composite \(x \circ p_C\colon C \to D\): \[ \const _x: C \xrightarrow {p_C} * \xrightarrow {x} D. \]

Remark 1.1.7. Observe that a category \(C\) is contractible if and only if there exists an absolute object \(x\colon * \to C\) such that the composite \(\const _x\colon C \to C\) is naturally isomorphic to the identity \(\id _C\colon C \to C\). A natural isomorphism \(H\colon \const _x \cong \id _C\) is called a contraction of \(C\) onto \(x\).

Agda Characterizing contractibility

contractible-to-contraction

Derived · checked against supplied interface

contractible-to-contraction : {C : CAT} → IsContractible C → Contraction C
Proof / implementation
contractible-to-contraction e = record
  { center = IsEquiv.inverse e
  ; contraction = invIso (IsEquiv.sectionIso e)

Products of categories

Next we introduce the product of two categories.

Axiom A.3 (Product of categories). The product of categories \(C\) and \(D\) is a category \(C\times D\) equipped with projection functors \(\pr _1\colon C\times D\to C\) and \(\pr _2\colon C\times D\to D\).

Its two projections are identified with \(\alpha \) and \(\beta \).

1.1.3 Coherences

In order for composition to behave as expected, we specify its units and associativity isomorphisms and their compatibility with natural isomorphisms.

Axiom A.4. For every functor \(f\), there is an identity natural isomorphism \(\id _f\colon f\cong f\). For parallel functors \(f,g,h\colon C\to D\), there is a composition functor \[ -\circ -\colon (g\cong h)\times (f\cong g)\longrightarrow (f\cong h). \] This composition is unital and associative, and the inverse functor supplies two-sided inverses, through specified natural isomorphisms of functors on the corresponding isomorphism animae. On objects these laws read \[ \id _g\circ \alpha \cong \alpha \cong \alpha \circ \id _f,\qquad (\gamma \circ \beta )\circ \alpha \cong \gamma \circ (\beta \circ \alpha ), \] \[ \alpha ^{-1}\circ \alpha \cong \id _f,\qquad \alpha \circ \alpha ^{-1}\cong \id _g. \]

Axiom A.5. Prewhiskering and postwhiskering preserve identity natural isomorphisms and vertical composition through specified natural isomorphisms of functors on the input isomorphism animae. For functors \(f,g,h\colon C\to D\), \(k\colon B\to C\) and \(u\colon D\to E\), these laws read \[ u\star \id _f\cong \id _{u\circ f},\qquad \id _f\star k\cong \id _{f\circ k}, \] \[ u\star (\tau \circ \sigma ) \cong (u\star \tau )\circ (u\star \sigma ),\qquad (\tau \circ \sigma )\star k \cong (\tau \star k)\circ (\sigma \star k), \] where \(\sigma \colon f\cong g\) and \(\tau \colon g\cong h\). Whiskering by an identity functor, by a composite, and in the two possible orders is compared using the unitors and associator of functor composition. For \(\sigma \colon f\cong g\), the identity laws are \[ \lambda _g\circ (\id _D\star \sigma ) \cong \sigma \circ \lambda _f,\qquad \rho _g\circ (\sigma \star \id _C) \cong \sigma \circ \rho _f. \] For additional functors \(l\colon A\to B\) and \(v\colon E\to F\), the composite laws are \begin {align*} \alpha _{g,u,v}\circ ((v\circ u)\star \sigma ) &\cong (v\star (u\star \sigma ))\circ \alpha _{f,u,v},\\ \alpha _{l,k,g}\circ ((\sigma \star k)\star l) &\cong (\sigma \star (k\circ l))\circ \alpha _{l,k,f}. \end {align*}

1.1.4 Terms

Let us collect some conventions for the term notation introduced above. An expression \(x:C\vdash f(x):D\) represents a functor \(C\to D\); the category \(D\) is fixed. For a functor \(\sigma \colon B\to C\), substitution gives the expression \(y:B\vdash f(\sigma (y)):D\), representing \(f\circ \sigma \). The unitality and associativity comparisons for substitution are those of composition of functors.

A natural isomorphism of expressions means a natural isomorphism of their whole functors. For example, \(x:C\vdash \alpha (x):f(x)\cong g(x)\) is a point of \((f\cong g)\), where \(f,g\colon C\to D\). A functor from another category to this fixed isomorphism anima is a different expression, with that anima as its target.

The notation is inspired by type-theoretic approaches to synthetic category theory, such as [RS17; GWB24]. Here substitution is composition of functors, and its laws are the specified isomorphisms. A functor and its term display are simply two representations of the same datum.
